企业和非营利机构领导者应认识暗黑模式，并尽量避开它造成的灰色地带。

合乎伦理的说服性设计与暗黑模式之间，界线在哪里？
3:1: Businesses should engage in conversations with IT, compliance, risk, and legal teams to review their privacy policy, and include in the discussion the customer/user experience designers and coders responsible for the company's user interface, as well as the marketers and advertisers responsible for sign-ups, checkout baskets, pricing, and promotions.
企业应让IT、合规、风险和法务团队展开对话，审查隐私政策；还应把负责公司用户界面的客户/用户体验设计师和程序员，以及负责注册、购物车、定价和促销的营销与广告人员纳入讨论。

这些团队中的任何一个或全部，都可能在制造或避免“数字欺骗”中发挥作用。

立法者和监管者正缓慢开始处理暗黑模式周围的模糊地带，最近的行动主要发生在州一级。

3月，加州总检察长宣布批准《加州消费者隐私法》下的补充规定，“确保消费者在寻求行使数据隐私权时不会受到迷惑或误导”。

这些规定旨在禁止暗黑模式，也就是禁止公司使用“令人困惑的语言或不必要步骤，例如迫使消费者点击多个页面，或听取不应退出的理由”。
5:0: As more states consider promulgating additional regulations, there is a need for greater accountability from within the business community.
随着更多州考虑颁布补充规定，商业界内部需要承担更大责任。
5:1: Dark patterns also can be addressed on a self-regulatory basis, but only if organizations hold themselves accountable, not just to legal requirements but also to industry best practices and standards.
暗黑模式也可以通过行业自律解决，但前提是组织不仅对法律要求负责，也对行业最佳实践和标准负责。

0:0: Although ethics classes are common around the world, scientists are unsure if their lessons can actually change behavior; evidence either way is weak, relying on contrived laboratory tests or sometimes unreliable self-reports.
虽然伦理课在世界各地很常见，科学家却不确定课程内容是否真能改变行为；支持或反对的证据都很薄弱，依赖人为设计的实验室测试或有时不可靠的自我报告。
0:1: But a new study published in Cognition found that, in at least one real-world situation, a single ethics lesson may have had lasting effects.
但发表在《认知》上的一项新研究发现，至少在一种现实情境中，一堂伦理课可能产生了持久影响。
1:0: The researchers investigated one class session's impact on eating meat.
研究人员考察了一节课对吃肉行为的影响。

研究合著者、加州大学河滨分校哲学家埃里克·施维茨格贝尔说，他们选择这一行为有三个原因：学生对此态度多变且不稳定，行为容易衡量，而且伦理学文献普遍认为少吃肉能减少环境破坏和动物痛苦，因此是好事。
1:2: Half of the students in four large philosophy classes read an article on the ethics of factory-farmed meat, optionally watched an 11-minute video on the topic and joined a 50-minute discussion.
四个大型哲学班中，一半学生阅读关于工厂化养殖肉类伦理的文章，可自愿观看11分钟相关视频，并参加50分钟讨论。
1:3: The other half focused on charitable giving instead.
另一半则学习慈善捐赠。

随后在学生不知情的情况下，研究人员分析了他们该学期匿名化的餐卡购买记录——近500名学生、约1.4万张小票。

另一组的购买比例则维持在52%。

“对这样小的干预来说，这其实是相当大的效果，”施维茨格贝尔说。

没有参与研究的宾夕法尼亚大学心理学家尼娜·施特罗明格说，她希望效果真实，却无法排除某个未知混杂变量。

她还指出，即使效果真实，也可能被另一次轻推逆转：“来得容易，去得也快。”

4:1: Second, the video may have had an emotional impact.
其次，视频可能产生情感影响。
4:2: Least rousing, he thinks, was rational argument, although his co-authors say reason might play a bigger role.
他认为最不起作用的是理性论证，不过合著者说理性也许发挥更大作用。
4:3: Now the researchers are probing the specific effects of teaching style, teaching assistants' eating habits and students' video exposure.
研究人员正在进一步探查教学风格、助教饮食习惯和学生观看视频各自的具体效果。
4:4: Meanwhile, Schwitzgebel-who had predicted no effect-will be eating his words.
与此同时，原本预测没有效果的施维茨格贝尔只好“收回自己的话”。

在当代文化中，与陌生人交谈——甚至只是看对方一眼——似乎都让人难以忍受。

高管心理教练乔恩·沃特曼认为，一个答案是恐惧。

我们害怕被拒绝，也怕自己无恶意的交往举动被误解成“古怪”。

我们害怕受到评判。

我们害怕打扰别人。

陌生人本来就与我们不熟悉，因此，与他们交谈时，我们比与朋友或熟人交谈更容易焦虑。

为了避免这种不安，我们转而求助于手机。

沃特曼说：“手机成了我们的安全毯。”

“它们像一副让我们安心的眼镜，保护我们不去面对那些被我们认为更危险的事。”

但一旦揭掉这块创可贴，把智能手机塞回口袋并抬起头，事情其实并没有那么令人难受。

在2011年的一次实验中，行为科学家尼古拉斯·埃普利和朱莉安娜·施罗德请通勤者做一件难以想象的事：主动开始交谈。

道理就是这么简单：与陌生人交谈能让你感觉自己与他人相连。

研究者想知道，伴随快乐而来的乐观态度和冒险倾向，是否会改变企业的投资方式。
0:6: So they compared U. S. cities' average happiness 【measured】 by Gallup polling with the investment activity of publicly traded firms in those areas. 【Sure】 enough, firms' investment and R&D intensity were correlated with the happiness of the area in which they were 【headquartered】.
于是，他们将盖洛普民调测得的美国城市平均幸福水平，与这些地区上市公司的投资活动作比较。果然，企业投资和研发强度与其总部所在地区的幸福水平相关。
0:7: But is it really happiness that's linked to investment, or could something else about happier cities 【explain】 why firms there spend more on R&D?
但与投资有关的真是快乐本身吗？或者，快乐城市的其他特征也能解释当地企业为什么在研发上花费更多？
0:8: To find out, the researchers controlled for various 【factors】 that might make firms more likely to invest - like size, industry, and sales - and for indicators that a place was 【desirable】 to live in, like growth in wages or population.
为了查明这一点，研究者控制了企业规模、行业和销售额等可能增加投资意愿的因素，也控制了工资或人口增长等反映地区宜居性的指标。
0:9: The link between happiness and investment generally 【held】 even after accounting for these things.
即使考虑了这些因素，快乐与投资之间的联系总体上仍然成立。
0:10: The correlation between happiness and investment was particularly strong for younger firms, which the authors 【attribute】 to "less codified decision making process" and the possible presence of "younger and less 【experienced】 managers who are more likely to be influenced by sentiment."
这种相关性在较年轻的企业中尤其强；作者将其归因于“较少制度化的决策过程”，以及可能存在的“更年轻、经验更少、容易受情绪影响的管理者”。
0:11: The relationship was 【also】 stronger in places where happiness was spread more 【equally】.
在幸福分布更均匀的地区，这种关系也更强。
0:12: Firms seem to invest more in places where most people are relatively happy, rather than in places with happiness inequality. 【While】 this doesn't prove that happiness causes firms to invest more or to take a longer-term view, the authors believe it at least 【hints】 at that possibility.
企业似乎更愿意在多数人都比较快乐的地区投资，而不是在幸福分布不均的地区投资。虽然这不能证明快乐导致企业增加投资或采取更长远的视角，作者认为，它至少暗示了这种可能性。
0:13: It's not hard to imagine that local culture and sentiment would help 【shape】 how executives think about the future.
不难想象，当地的文化与情绪会影响管理者对未来的思考。
0:14: "It surely seems plausible that happy people would be more forward-thinking and creative and 【lean towards】 R&D more than the average," said one researcher.
一位研究者说：“快乐的人会更有前瞻性、更富创造力，也比一般人更倾向投入研发，这的确是合理的推测。”

0:0: People have speculated for centuries about a future without work.
几个世纪以来，人们一直在设想一个无需工作的未来。
0:1: Today is no different, with academics, writers, and activists once again 【warning】 that technology is replacing human workers.
今天也不例外，学者、作家和社会活动人士再次警告：技术正在取代人类劳动者。
0:2: Some imagine that the coming work-free world will be defined by 【inequality】: A few wealthy people will own all the capital, and the masses will struggle in an impoverished wasteland.
有人想象，未来没有工作的世界将以不平等为特征：少数富人拥有全部资本，而大众在贫困荒原中挣扎。
0:3: A different and not mutually exclusive 【prediction】 holds that the future will be a wasteland of a different sort, one 【characterized】 by purposelessness: Without jobs to give their lives 【meaning】, people will simply become lazy and depressed. 【Indeed】, today's unemployed don't seem to be having a great time.
另一种并不与前一观点互相排斥的预测认为，未来将是另一种荒原，其特征是失去目标：没有工作赋予生活意义，人们会变得懒散、沮丧。事实上，今天的失业者似乎也过得并不好。
0:4: One Gallup poll found that 20 percent of Americans who have been unemployed for at least a year report having depression, double the rate for 【working】 Americans.
一项盖洛普民调发现，失业至少一年的美国人中有百分之二十报告患有抑郁症，是有工作者的两倍。
0:5: Also, some research suggests that the 【explanation】 for rising rates of mortality, mental-health problems, and addiction 【among】 poorly-educated, middle-aged people is a shortage of well-paid jobs.
还有研究认为，受教育程度较低的中年人死亡率、心理健康问题和成瘾发生率上升，原因是缺少报酬丰厚的工作。
0:6: Perhaps this is why many 【worry about】 the agonizing dullness of a jobless future.
这或许就是许多人担心，无工作的未来会让人无聊得难以忍受的原因。
0:7: But it doesn't 【necessarily】 follow from findings like these that a world without work would be filled with unease.
但这些发现不一定能推出一个结论：没有工作的世界必然充满不安。
0:8: Such visions are based on the 【downsides】 of being unemployed in a society built on the concept of employment.
这些设想依据的是，在一个围绕就业观念构建的社会中，失业会带来的负面影响。
0:9: In the 【absence】 of work, a society designed with other ends in mind could 【yield】 strikingly different circumstances for the future of labor and leisure.
如果没有工作，一个以其他目标来设计的社会，也可能为劳动与休闲的未来创造截然不同的条件。
0:10: Today, the 【virtue】 of work may be a bit overblown.
如今，工作的好处或许被夸大了一点。
0:11: "Many jobs are boring, degrading, unhealthy, and a waste of human potential," says John Danaher, a lecturer at the National University of Ireland in Galway.
爱尔兰国立大学戈尔韦分校讲师约翰·达纳赫说：“许多工作无聊、有损尊严、不利健康，还浪费人的潜能。”
0:12: These days, because leisure time is relatively 【scarce】 for most workers, people use their free time to counterbalance the intellectual and emotional 【demands】 of their jobs.
现在，大多数劳动者的闲暇比较稀少，因此人们用空闲时间来抵消工作对智力和情感的要求。
0:13: "When I come home from a hard day's work, I often feel 【tired】," Danaher says, adding, "In a world in which I don't have to work, I might feel rather different" - perhaps different enough to throw himself 【into】 a hobby or a passion project with the intensity usually reserved for 【professional】 matters.
达纳赫说：“辛苦工作一天回家后，我常觉得疲惫。”他接着说：“在一个我不必工作的世界里，我的感受可能会很不同。”或许不同到足以让他把通常留给专业事务的精力，全心投入爱好或自己热爱的项目。

0:0: Why do people read negative Internet comments and do other things that will obviously be painful?
人们为什么会去看网上的负面评论，或做其他明显会让自己难受的事？
0:1: Because humans have an inherent need to 【resolve】 uncertainty, according to a recent study in Psychological Science.
《心理科学》最近一项研究认为，这是因为人类有一种消除不确定性的内在需求。
0:2: The new research reveals that the need to know is so strong that people will 【seek】 to satisfy their curiosity even when it is clear the answer will 【hurt】.
新研究表明，想知道答案的需求如此强烈，即使明知答案会伤害自己，人们也会设法满足好奇心。
0:3: In a series of four experiments, behavioral scientists at the University of Chicago and the Wisconsin School of Business tested students' willingness to 【expose】 themselves to unpleasant stimuli in an effort to satisfy curiosity.
在四组实验中，芝加哥大学与威斯康星商学院的行为科学家测试了学生为了满足好奇心，愿意让自己接触不愉快刺激的程度。
0:4: For one 【trial】, each participant was shown a pile of pens that the researcher claimed were from a previous experiment.
在一次试验中，每位参与者都看到一堆笔，研究者称这些笔来自之前的实验。
0:5: The twist?
其中有什么意外之处？
0:6: Half of the pens would 【deliver】 an electric shock when clicked.
一半的笔按下后会给人电击。
0:7: Twenty-seven students were told which pens were electrified; another twenty-seven were told only that some were electrified. 【When】 left alone in the room, the students who did not know which ones would shock them clicked more pens and incurred more shocks than the students who knew what would 【happen】.
二十七名学生被告知哪些笔带电，另外二十七人只知道有些笔带电。独自留在房间后，不知道哪些笔会电击的学生按了更多笔、遭受更多电击，比知道会发生什么的学生更多。
0:8: Subsequent experiments reproduced this effect with other stimuli, 【such as】 the sound of fingernails on a chalkboard and photographs of disgusting insects.
后续实验使用其他刺激也重复出了这一效果，例如指甲划黑板的声音，以及令人恶心的昆虫照片。
0:9: The drive to 【discover】 is deeply rooted in humans, much the same as the basic drives for 【food】 or shelter, says Christopher Hsee of the University of Chicago.
芝加哥大学的奚恺元表示，探索未知的驱动力根植于人性，正如追求食物或住所的基本需求一样。
0:10: Curiosity is often considered a good instinct - it can 【lead to】 new scientific advances, for instance - but sometimes such 【inquiry】 can backfire.
好奇心常被视为好的本能，例如它能带来科学新进展；但有时，这种探究也会适得其反。
0:11: The insight that curiosity can drive you to do 【self-destructive】 things is a profound one.
好奇心会驱使你做出自我伤害的事情，这是一项深刻的认识。
0:12: Unhealthy curiosity is possible to 【resist】, however.
不过，不健康的好奇心是可以抵制的。
0:13: In a final experiment, participants who were encouraged to 【predict】 how they would feel after viewing an unpleasant picture were less likely to 【choose】 to see such an image.
在最后一项实验中，参与者若被鼓励先预测看过不愉快图片后会有什么感受，就较少选择去看这些图片。
0:14: These results suggest that imagining the 【outcome】 of following through on one's curiosity ahead of time can help determine 【whether】 it is worth the endeavor.
结果表明，事先想象满足好奇心会产生什么结果，有助于判断这件事是否值得去做。
0:15: "Thinking about long-term 【consequences】 is key to reducing the possible negative effects of curiosity," Hsee says.
奚恺元说：“思考长期后果，是减少好奇心可能带来的负面影响的关键。”
0:16: In other words, don't read online comments.
换句话说，不要去看网上评论。

0:0: Weighing yourself regularly is a wonderful way to stay aware of any significant weight fluctuations. 【However】, when done too often, this habit can sometimes hurt more than it 【helps】.
定期称重是留意体重明显波动的好办法。不过，如果称得过于频繁，这个习惯有时会弊大于利。

这不利于我的整体健身目标。

我的体重增加来自肌肉量增长，但我只想着降低秤上的数字，便改变了训练计划。

这与实现目标所需要的训练方式相冲突。

我还发现，每天称重无法准确体现我在健身房付出的努力和取得的进步。

改变训练计划后，大约需要三周到一个月，才会看到体重出现明显变化。
0:7: The most 【immediate】 changes will be observed in skill level, strength and inches lost.
最先看得见的变化会体现在技能水平、力量，以及身体围度的缩减上。
0:8: For these 【reasons】, I stopped weighing myself every day and switched to a bimonthly weighing schedule 【instead】.
由于这些原因，我不再每天称重，改为每月两次。

减重不是我的目标，因此每周追踪体重对我并不那么重要。

每隔一周称一次，能让我观察明显的体重变化，并判断其原因。

这能告诉我是否需要调整训练计划。
0:12: I use my bimonthly weigh-in 【results】 to get information about my nutrition as well.
我也用每月两次的称重结果来了解自己的营养状况。

如果训练强度不变，我却总是饥饿、体重不断下降，这就说明需要增加每天的热量摄入。
0:14: The 【decision】 to stop weighing myself every day has done wonders for my overall health, fitness and well-being.
停止每天称重的决定，极大改善了我的整体健康、体能和身心状态。
0:15: I'm experiencing increased zeal for working out since I no longer carry the burden of a 【disappointing】 morning weigh-in.
不再背负早晨称重结果令人失望的负担后，我对锻炼更有热情了。
0:16: I've also experienced greater success in achieving my specific fitness goals, 【because】 I'm training according to those goals, not the numbers on a scale.
实现具体健身目标也更顺利，因为我按照那些目标训练，而不是按照秤上的数字训练。

与其痴迷体重秤，不如关注自己的外观、感受、衣服是否合身，以及整体精力水平。

0:0: Being a good parent is, of course, what every parent would like to be.

一个安静、守规矩的孩子，适合的教养方式可能不同于较年幼的弟妹。幸运的是，另一类父母比较容易描述：有耐心的父母。

各个年龄的孩子，都能从有耐心的教养中受益。

0:5: Sometimes parents get exhausted and frustrated and are unable to maintain a 【tolerant】 and composed style with their kids.
有时父母会疲惫、沮丧，无法继续宽容、冷静地对待孩子。
0:6: I understand this.
我理解这一点。
0:7: You're only human, and sometimes your kids can 【push】 you just a little too far.
你毕竟只是普通人，而孩子有时会把你逼得稍微过了头。
0:8: And then the 【inevitable】 happens: You lose your patience and either scream at your kids or say something that was a bit too 【harsh】 and does nobody any good.
于是，难免的事情发生了：你失去耐心，不是冲孩子大喊，就是说了过于严厉、对谁都没好处的话。

你希望时光倒流、重新来过；我们都经历过。可是，即便这很常见，也要记住：一瞬间的疲惫，可能让你对孩子说出令自己长期后悔的话。
0:10: This may not only do damage to your relationship with your child but also 【affect】 your child's self-esteem.
这不仅可能伤害亲子关系，还会影响孩子的自尊。
0:11: If you consistently lose your 【cool】 with your kids, then you are inadvertently modeling a lack of emotional control for your kids.
如果你总对孩子失去冷静，就在无意中向孩子示范缺乏情绪控制的行为。
0:12: We are all becoming increasingly aware of the 【importance】 of modeling tolerance and patience for the younger generation.
我们越来越意识到，给年轻一代示范宽容与耐心的重要性。
0:13: This is a skill that will help them all throughout life.
这种能力将使他们终身受益。
0:14: In fact, the ability to emotionally regulate or maintain emotional control when 【confronted】 by stress is one of the most important of all life's skills.
事实上，面对压力时能调节情绪、保持情绪控制，是人生最重要的能力之一。

当然，面对孩子时时时刻刻保持耐心，非常困难。
0:16: A more practical goal is to try, to the best of your ability, to be as tolerant and composed as you can when faced with 【trying】 situations involving your children.
一个更实际的目标是：遇到与孩子有关的棘手情况时，尽自己所能，尽量宽容、冷静。
0:17: I can promise you this: As a result of working toward this goal. you and your children will benefit and 【emerge】 from stressful moments feeling better physically and emotionally.
我可以向你保证：朝这个目标努力，会让你和孩子受益，走出压力时刻后，身体与情绪都会感觉更好。

0:0: It's not difficult to set targets for staff.

0:2: Most work-related behaviors have multiple components. 【Emphasize】 one and the others become distorted.
大多数工作行为都包含多个部分；过分强调其中一个，其他部分就会扭曲。
0:3: Travel on a London bus and you'll 【quickly】 see how this works with drivers.
乘一趟伦敦公交车，很快就能从司机身上看出这一机制。

会有人不付钱就上车吗？

有查票员检查乘客是否付费吗？

闯红灯又如何？

公交车闯红灯的频率几乎和骑车人一样高。

人们抱怨公交晚点、班次少；于是公交车辆和专用车道增加了，司机也按耗时长短获得奖励或受到处罚。

你注意过吗，有时航班起飞晚了一小时，却仍能准时抵达？

一小时的航程，现在被列为两小时。

0:0: Harlan Coben believes that if you're a writer, you'll find the time; and that if you can't find the time, then writing isn't a priority and you're not a writer.
哈兰·科本认为，如果你是作家，就会找到时间；如果找不到时间，说明写作不是优先事项，你也就不是作家。
0:1: For him writing is a 【normal】 job-a job like any other.
对他来说，写作是一份普通工作，和其他工作一样。
0:2: He has 【compared】 it with plumbing, pointing out that a plumber doesn't wake up and say that he can't work with pipes today. 【If】, like most writers these days, you're holding down a job to pay the bills, it's not 【easy】 to find the time to write.
他把写作比作管道维修，指出水管工不会醒来就说今天没法碰管道。如果你和如今大多数作家一样，必须另做一份工作来支付账单，就不容易挤出时间写作。
0:3: But it's not impossible.
但这并非不可能。

它需要决心与专心致志。记住，大多数畅销书作者开始写作时，也在做其他事情谋生。
0:5: And today, even writers who are fairly 【well-known】 often have to do other work to 【supplement】 their writing income.
今天，即使相当知名的作家，也常得做其他工作来补足写作收入。
0:6: As Harlan Coben has suggested, it's a 【question】 of priorities.
正如科本所说，这归根结底是优先顺序的问题。
0:7: To make writing a priority, you'll have to 【sacrifice】 some of your day-to-day activities and some things you really enjoy.
要把写作放在优先位置，就得牺牲一些日常活动，以及一些真正喜欢的事情。
0:8: Depending on your 【interests】 and your lifestyle, that might mean spending less time watching television or listening to music, though some people can write 【while】 they listen to music.
根据兴趣与生活方式，这可能意味着少看电视、少听音乐，虽然有人能一边听音乐一边写作。
0:9: You might have to 【cut down on】 the amount of exercise or sport you do.
你也许得减少运动或体育活动的量。
0:10: You'll have to make social media an 【occasional】 activity rather than a daily, time-consuming 【habit】.
社交媒体必须变成偶尔的活动，而不是每天耗时的习惯。
0:11: There'll probably have to be less socialising with your friends and less time with your family.
你可能还得减少与朋友社交，以及陪伴家人的时间。
0:12: It's a 【tough】 learning curve and it won't always make you popular.
这是艰难的适应过程，也未必总让你讨人喜欢。
0:13: There's just one thing you should try to keep at least some time for, 【in addition to】 your writing-and that's reading.
除了写作，还有一件事应尽量留出一些时间：阅读。
0:14: Any writer needs to read as much and as widely as they can; it's the one 【indispensable】 supporter-something you can't do without.
任何作家都需要尽可能多、尽可能广地阅读；这是不可或缺的支持，是离不开的东西。
0:16: The older you get, the 【quicker】 it seems to go.
年龄越大，越觉得它流逝得快。
0:17: We need to use it as carefully and as 【productively】 as we can, that means prioritising our activities so that we spend most time on the things we really want to do.
我们应尽可能谨慎且有成效地使用时间，也就是为活动排出优先顺序，把大部分时间用在真正想做的事情上。
0:18: If you're a writer, that means- 【above all】 writing.

0:0: Some Old Truths to Help You Overcome Tough Times
帮助你度过艰难时期的一些老道理。
1:0: Unfortunately, life is not a bed of roses.
遗憾的是，生活并非一帆风顺。
1:1: We are going through life facing sad experiences.
人生路上，我们不断面对令人伤心的经历。
1:2: Moreover, we are grieving various kinds of loss: a friendship, a romantic relationship or a house.
而且，我们会为各种失去而哀伤：一段友谊、一份爱情，或一所房子。
1:3: Hard times may hold you down at what usually seems like the most inopportune time, but you should remember that they won't last forever.
困难也许会在最不合时宜的时候压住你，但要记住，它们不会永远持续。
1:4: When our time of mourning is over, we press forward, stronger with a greater understanding and respect for life.
哀伤时期结束后，我们会带着对生活更深的理解和尊重，更坚强地继续前进。
1:5: Furthermore, these losses make us mature and eventually move us toward future opportunities for growth and happiness.
此外，这些失去让我们成熟，并最终带我们走向未来成长与幸福的机会。
1:6: I want to share these old truths I've learned along the way.
我想分享这些一路走来学到的老道理。
2:0: Fear is both useful and harmful.
恐惧既有用，也有害。
2:1: This normal human reaction is used to protect us by signaling danger and preparing us to deal with it.
这种正常的人类反应会提示危险、让我们准备应对，从而保护我们。
2:2: Unfortunately, people create inner barriers with a help of exaggerating fears.
遗憾的是，人们会通过夸大恐惧，给自己制造内心的障碍。
2:3: My favorite actor Will Smith once said, "Fear is not real.
我喜欢的演员威尔·史密斯曾说：“恐惧不是真实的。
2:4: It is a product of thoughts you create.
它是你所创造的想法的产物。
2:5: Do not misunderstand me.
别误会我的意思。
2:8: I do completely agree that fears are just the product of our luxuriant imagination.
我完全赞同：恐惧只是我们丰富想象力的产物。
3:0: If you are surrounded by problems and cannot stop thinking about the past, try to focus on the present moment.
如果你被问题包围、无法停止回想过去，试着专注当下。
3:1: Many of us are weighed down by the past or anxious about the future.
我们很多人被过去压得喘不过气，或为未来焦虑。
3:2: You may feel guilt over your past, but you are poisoning the present with the things and circumstances you cannot change.
你也许为过去内疚，却正在用那些无法改变的事情和处境破坏现在。
3:3: Value the present moment and remember how fortunate you are to be alive.
珍惜当下，记住活着本身有多幸运。
3:4: Enjoy the beauty of the world around and keep the eyes open to see the possibilities before you.
欣赏周围世界的美，睁开眼看看面前的可能性。
3:5: Happiness is not a point of future and not a moment from the past, but a mindset that can be designed into the present.
幸福不是未来的某个时间点，也不是过去的某一瞬，而是可以融入当下的一种心态。
4:0: Sometimes it is easy to feel bad because you are going through tough times.
有时，经历困难很容易让人心情低落。
4:1: You can be easily caught up by life problems that you forget to pause and appreciate the things you have.
生活中的问题可能把你卷进去，让你忘记停下来珍惜已经拥有的东西。
4:2: Only strong people prefer to smile and value their life instead of crying and complaining about something.
坚强的人更愿意微笑、珍视自己的生活，而不是为某件事哭泣和抱怨。
5:0: No matter how isolated you might feel and how serious the situation is, you should always remember that you are not alone.
不管你觉得多孤单、情况有多严重，都要记住你并不孤单。
5:1: Try to keep in mind that almost everyone respects and wants to help you if you are trying to make a good change in your life, especially your dearest and nearest people.
记住，只要你努力让生活变好，几乎人人都会尊重你并愿意帮助你，尤其是最亲近的人。
5:2: You may have a circle of friends who provide constant good humor, help and companionship.
你的朋友圈也许能持续提供好心情、帮助和陪伴。
5:3: If you have no friends or relatives, try to participate in several online communities, full of people who are always willing to share advice and encouragement.
如果没有朋友或亲人，可以加入一些网络群体，那里有许多愿意分享建议与鼓励的人。
6:0: Today many people find it difficult to trust their own opinion and seek balance by gaining objectivity from external sources.
如今，许多人难以相信自己的看法，试图从外部获得客观性，以此寻找平衡。
6:1: This way you devalue your opinion and show that you are incapable of managing your own life.
这样做会贬低自己的意见，也表明你无法管理自己的人生。
6:2: When you are struggling to achieve something important you should believe in yourself and be sure that your decision is the best.
努力实现重要目标时，应相信自己，并对自己的决定有信心。
6:3: You live in your skin, think your own thoughts, have your own values and make your own choices.
你活在自己的身体里，思考自己的想法，拥有自己的价值观，也作出自己的选择。

0:0: Act Your Shoe Size, Not Your Age
按鞋码而非年龄行事——向孩子学习快乐。
1:0: As adults, it seems that we are constantly pursuing happiness, often with mixed results.
作为成年人，我们似乎总在追求幸福，结果却有好有坏。
1:1: Yet children appear to have it down to an art - and for the most part they don't need self-help books or therapy.
孩子似乎已将这件事掌握得炉火纯青，而且多数时候并不需要自助书或心理治疗。
1:2: Instead, they look after their wellbeing instinctively, and usually more effectively than we do as grownups.
他们本能地照顾自己的身心状态，通常比成人更有效。
1:3: Perhaps it's time to learn a few lessons from them.
也许是时候向他们学几课了。
2:0: What does a child do when he's sad?
孩子难过时会做什么？
2:1: He cries.
他会哭。
2:2: When he's angry?
生气时呢？
2:3: He shouts.
他会喊。
2:4: Scared?
害怕时呢？
2:5: Probably a bit of both.
也许哭和喊都有一点。
2:6: As we grow up, we learn to control our emotions so they are manageable and don't dictate our behaviours, which is in many ways a good thing.
长大后，我们学会控制情绪，使它们可管理、不至于支配行为；从许多方面看，这是一件好事。
2:7: But too often we take this process too far and end up suppressing emotions, especially negative ones.
但我们常常走得太远，最后变成压抑情绪，尤其负面情绪。
2:8: That's about as effective as brushing dirt under a carpet and can even make us ill.
这就像把灰尘扫到地毯下面一样无效，甚至会让人生病。
2:9: What we need to do is find a way to acknowledge and express what we feel appropriately, and then - again, like children - move on.
我们需要找到适当承认并表达自己感受的方法，然后像孩子一样继续向前。
3:0: A couple of Christmases ago, my youngest stepdaughter, who was nine years old at the time, got a Superman T-shirt for Christmas.
几年前的一个圣诞节，我当时九岁的最小继女得到了一件超人T恤。
3:1: It cost less than a fiver but she was overjoyed, and couldn't stop talking about it.
它不到五英镑，却让她欣喜若狂，谈个不停。
3:2: Too often we believe that a new job, bigger house or better car will be the magic silver bullet that will allow us to finally be content, but the reality is these things have very little lasting impact on our happiness levels.
我们常以为，新工作、大房子或更好的车会是让我们终于满足的万能法宝；但事实是，这些东西对长期幸福水平的影响很小。
3:3: Instead, being grateful for small things every day is a much better way to improve wellbeing.
相比之下，每天感恩小事是改善身心状态的更好办法。
4:0: Have you ever noticed how much children laugh?
你注意过孩子笑得有多频繁吗？
4:1: If we adults could indulge in a bit of silliness and giggling, we would reduce the stress hormones in our bodies, increase good hormones like endorphins, improve blood flow to our hearts and even have a greater chance of fighting off infection.
成人若也偶尔傻气一下、咯咯笑，体内的压力激素会减少，内啡肽等有益激素会增加，流向心脏的血液循环会改善，甚至更有机会抵抗感染。
4:2: All of which would, of course, have a positive effect on our happiness levels.
当然，这些都会积极影响我们的幸福感。
5:0: The problem with being a grownup is that there's an awful lot of serious stuff to deal with - work, mortgage payments, figuring out what to cook for dinner.
成人的问题是有太多严肃事务要处理：工作、房贷，还要想晚饭做什么。
5:1: But as adults we also have the luxury of being able to control our own diaries and it's important that we schedule in time to enjoy the things we love.
但成年人也有掌控自己日程的便利，因此安排时间享受喜爱的事情很重要。
5:2: Those things might be social, sporting, creative or completely random (dancing around the living room, anyone?) - it doesn't matter, so long as they're enjoyable, and not likely to have negative side effects, such as drinking too much alcohol or going on a wild spending spree if you're on a tight budget.
这些事情可以是社交、运动、创作，也可以完全随兴，例如在客厅跳舞；只要令人愉快，又不带来酗酒或在预算紧张时疯狂购物等负面影响，做什么都可以。
6:0: Having said all of the above, it's important to add that we shouldn't try too hard to be happy.
说完上述这些，还必须补充一点：不应过分努力追求快乐。
6:1: Scientists tell us this can backfire and actually have a negative impact on our wellbeing.
科学家告诉我们，这可能适得其反，损害身心状态。
6:2: As the Chinese philosopher Chuang Tzu is reported to have said: "Happiness is the absence of striving for happiness."
据说，中国哲学家庄子曾说：“幸福就是不再费力追求幸福。”
6:3: And in that, once more, we need to look to the example of our children, to whom happiness is not a goal but a natural byproduct of the way they live.
在这一点上，我们又应向孩子学习：对他们而言，快乐不是目标，而是生活方式自然带来的结果。

0:3: The decline in American manufacturing is a common refrain, particularly from Donald Trump.
美国制造业衰退是一种常见论调，尤其经常出自唐纳德·特朗普之口。

他在福克斯新闻为自己墨西哥制造的服装品牌辩护时说：“我们已经不制造任何东西了。”

家族企业Wolverine Coil Spring总裁杰伊·邓韦尔说：“他们更难找，而且手上已有工作邀请。他们也许正进入劳动力市场，但已经被其他发展得和制造业同样好的行业挖走。”

邓韦尔开始让高中倒数第二学年的学生参观工厂，使他们接触工厂文化。

罗斯让三名社区大学学生参加工作实践项目，起薪每小时十三美元，两年后升至十七美元。

变压器厂的工作台旁，年轻的贾森·斯滕奎斯特正尝试组装铜线圈，又遇到两名访客，显得有些慌张。

但为了吸引年轻工人，制造商还得跨过一个大障碍：他们的父母经历过大萧条以来最严重的美国经济衰退，劝他们别进工厂。

千禧一代“记得父亲和母亲都被裁员。

他们把这归咎于制造业衰退。”密歇根西部商业发展机构The Right Place的负责人比尔吉特·克洛斯说。

经济复苏开始时，用工短缺首先出现在高技能工种。

如今，中等技能层级也开始出现短缺。

“麦当劳和其他不太需要技能的地方，有足够的人来填补岗位。

问题就在中间这一层的缺口。”

大急流城社区学院的朱莉·帕克斯指出，吸引千禧一代进入制造业的另一关键，是工作与生活的平衡。

父母辈愿意长时间工作，但年轻人看重灵活性。

0:0: Five ways to make conversation with anyone
与任何人交谈的五种方法。
1:0: Conversations are links, which means when you have a conversation with a new person a link gets formed and every conversation you have after that moment will strengthen the link.
谈话就是联结：与新认识的人交谈会建立联系，而此后的每次交谈都会加强这种联系。
1:1: You meet new people every day: the grocery worker, the cab driver, new people at work or the security guard at the door.
你每天都会遇见新的人：杂货店员工、出租车司机、新同事，或门口的保安。
1:2: Simply starting a conversation with them will form a link.
只要与他们开始交谈，就能建立联结。
1:3: Here are five simple ways that you can make the first move and start a conversation with strangers.
下面有五种简单方法，帮助你迈出第一步，与陌生人开始交谈。
2:0: Suppose you are in a room with someone you don't know and something within you says "I want to talk with this person" - this is something that mostly happens with all of us.
假设你与一个不认识的人同处一室，心里想着“我想跟这个人说话”——多数人都会遇到这种情况。
2:1: You wanted to say something - the first word - but it just won't come out, it feels like it is stuck somewhere.
你想说点什么、说出第一个词，但它就是出不来，好像卡在某处。
2:2: I know the feeling and here is my advice: just get it out.
我懂这种感觉，我的建议是：先把话说出口。
2:3: Just think: what is the worst that could happen?
想一想，最坏能发生什么？
2:4: They won't talk with you?
他们不跟你说话？
2:5: Well, they are not talking with you now!
可他们现在本来就没有跟你说话！
2:6: I truly believe that once you get that first word out everything else will just flow.
我确实相信，只要说出第一个词，后面就会顺畅起来。
2:7: So keep it simple: "Hi", "Hey"or "Hello" - do the best you can to gather all of the enthusiasm and energy you can, put on a big smile and say "Hi".
因此，简单一点就好：“嗨”“你好”都可以；尽量调动热情与精力，露出灿烂的微笑，说声“嗨”。
3:0: It is a problem all of us face; you have limited time with the person that you want to talk with and you want to make this talk memorable.
我们都面对一个问题：与想交谈的人相处时间有限，却又想让谈话令人难忘。
3:1: Honestly, if we got stuck in the rut of "hi", "hello", "how are you?" and "what is going on?", you will fail to give the initial jolt to the conversation that can make it so memorable.
说实话，如果困在“嗨”“你好”“你好吗”“最近怎么样”这些老套开场里，就无法给谈话带来那一下让人记住的触动。
3:2: So don't be afraid to ask more personal questions.
所以，不必害怕问一些更个人化的问题。
3:3: Trust me, you'll be surprised to see how much people are willing to share if you just ask.
相信我，只要开口问，你会惊讶于人们愿意分享多少事情。
4:0: When you meet a person for the first time, make an effort to find the things which you and that person have in common so that you can build the conversation from that point.
第一次见面时，努力找出你与对方的共同点，以此作为交谈的起点。
4:1: When you start conversation from there and then move outwards, you'll find all of a sudden that the conversation becomes a lot easier.
从共同点开始，再逐渐扩展，你会突然发现谈话容易得多了。
5:0: Imagine you are pouring your heart out to someone and they are just busy on their phone, and if you ask for their attention you get the response "I can multitask".
想象一下：你正在向某人倾诉，对方却只顾手机；你请他专心听，他还回答“我能同时做多件事”。
5:1: So when someone tries to communicate with you, just be in that communication wholeheartedly.
因此，有人尝试与你交流时，就全心投入这次交流。
5:2: Make eye contact.
与对方目光接触。
5:3: Trust me, eye contact is where all the magic happens.
相信我，目光接触正是产生奇妙联结的地方。
5:4: When you make eye contact, you can feel the conversation.
目光接触时，你能感受到谈话中的交流。
6:0: You all came into a conversation where you first met the person, but after some time you may have met again and have forgotten their name.
大家都经历过：第一次谈话时认识了一个人，过些时候再见，却忘了对方的名字。
6:1: Isn't that awkward!
这不是很尴尬吗！
6:2: So, remember the little details of the people you met or you talked with; perhaps the places they have been to, the places they want to go, the things they like, the things they hate - whatever you talk about.
因此，记住见过或聊过的人身上的小细节：去过哪里、想去哪里、喜欢什么、讨厌什么，谈到什么都可以。
6:3: When you remember such things you can automatically become investor in their wellbeing.
记住这些事情，你自然会成为关心对方过得好不好的人。
6:4: So they feel a responsibility to you to keep that relationship going.
这样，他们也会觉得有责任维系与你的关系。
6:6: Five amazing ways that you can make conversation with almost anyone.
五种很棒的方法，让你能与几乎任何人交谈。
6:7: Every person is a really good book to read, or to have a conversation with!
每个人都是一本值得读的好书，也是值得交谈的对象！

0:3: In choosing a new home, Camille McClain's kids have a single demand: a backyard.
选择新家时，卡米尔·麦克莱恩的孩子们只有一个要求：后院。
0:4: McClain's little ones aren't the only kids who have an opinion when it comes to housing, and in many cases youngsters' views weigh heavily on parents' real estate decisions, according to a 2018 Harris Poll survey of more than 2,000 U. S. adults.
并非只有麦克莱恩的孩子对住房有意见；2018年一项覆盖两千多名美国成年人的哈里斯民调显示，许多家庭中，孩子的看法会显著影响父母的房产决定。
0:5: While more families buck an older-generation proclivity to leave kids in the dark about real estate decisions, realty agents and psychologists have mixed views about the financial, personal and long-term effects kids' opinions may have.
越来越多家庭不再沿袭老一代不让孩子了解房产决策的习惯，但房产经纪人与心理学家对孩子意见可能带来的财务、个人及长期影响，看法不一。
0:6: The idea of involving children in a big decision is a great idea because it can help them feel a sense of control and ownership in what can be an overwhelming process, said Ryan Hooper, clinical psychologist in Chicago.
芝加哥临床心理学家瑞安·胡珀说，让孩子参与重大决定是好主意，因为在一个可能令人难以承受的过程中，这能让他们获得控制感与主人翁感。
0:7: "Children may face serious difficulties in coping with significant moves, especially if it removes them from their current school or support system," he said.
他说：“孩子应对重大搬迁可能非常困难，尤其当搬迁让他们离开现有学校或支持系统时。”
0:8: Greg Jaroszewski, real estate broker with Gagliardo Realty Associates, said he's not convinced that kids should be involved in selecting a home - but their opinions should be considered in regards to proximity to friends and social activities, if possible.
Gagliardo Realty Associates的房产经纪人格雷格·雅罗谢夫斯基说，他并不确信应让孩子参与选房，但在可能的情况下，应考虑离朋友和社交活动近不近等与孩子有关的意见。
0:9: Younger children should feel like they're choosing their home - without actually getting a choice in the matter, said Adam Bailey, real estate attorney based in New York.
纽约房产律师亚当·贝利说，较小的孩子应该感觉自己在选择新家，但实际上不让他们作决定。
0:10: Asking them questions about what they like about the backyard of a potential home will make them feel like they're being included in the decision-making process, Bailey said.
贝利说，问孩子喜欢候选住房后院的什么地方，会让他们觉得自己被纳入决策过程。
0:11: Many of the aspects of homebuying aren't a consideration for children, said Tracey Hampson, a real estate agent based in Santa Clarita, Calif.
加利福尼亚州圣克拉丽塔房产经纪人特蕾西·汉普森说，孩子不会考虑买房的许多方面。
0:12: And placing too much emphasis on their opinions can ruin a fantastic home purchase.
而过分强调他们的意见，可能毁掉一笔很好的房产交易。
0:13: "Speaking with your children before you make a real estate decision is wise, but I wouldn't base the purchasing decision solely on their opinions."
“作出房产决定之前和孩子谈谈是明智的，但我不会只凭他们的意见来决定购买。”
0:15: The other issue is that many children - especially older ones - may base their real state knowledge on HGTV shows, said Aaron Norris of The Norris Group in Riverside, Calif.
加利福尼亚州里弗赛德Norris Group的艾伦·诺里斯说，另一个问题是，许多孩子，尤其较年长者，可能从HGTV节目中形成房产知识。
0:16: "They love Chip and Joanna Gaines just as much as the rest of us," he said.
他说：“他们和我们其他人一样，喜欢奇普与乔安娜·盖恩斯。”
0:17: "HGTV has seriously changed how people view real estate.
“HGTV极大改变了人们看待房产的方式。
0:18: It's not shelter, it's a lifestyle.
它不只是住所，而是一种生活方式。
0:19: With that mindset change come some serious money consequences."
这种观念变化还伴随着严重的财务后果。”
0:20: Kids tend to get stuck in the features and the immediate benefits to them personally, Norris said.
诺里斯说，孩子容易只盯住房屋特色，以及自己马上能获得的好处。
0:21: Parents need to remind their children that their needs and desires may change over time, said Julie Gurner, a real estate analyst with FitSmallBusiness.com.
FitSmallBusiness.com房产分析师朱莉·格纳说，父母需要提醒孩子，他们的需要与愿望会随时间改变。
0:22: "Their opinions can change tomorrow," Gurner said.
格纳说：“他们的意见可能明天就变了。”
0:23: "Harsh as it may be to say, that decision should likely not be made contingent on a child's opinions, but rather made for them with great consideration into what home can meet their needs best-and give them an opportunity to customize it a bit and make it their own."
“尽管说起来严厉，但这个决定很可能不应取决于孩子的意见，而应替他们作出：充分考虑什么住房最能满足他们的需要，再给他们一点个性化布置的机会，让新家成为自己的家。”
0:24: This advice is more relevant now than ever before, even as more parents want to embrace the ideas of their children, despite the current housing crunch.
即使在当前住房紧张、更多父母想接纳孩子想法的情况下，这项建议也比以往更切题。

0:0: Five Ways to Win Over Everyone in the Office
赢得办公室所有人支持的五种方法。
1:0: Is it possible to like everyone in your office?
你能喜欢办公室里的每个人吗？
1:1: Think about how tough it is to get together 15 people, much less 50, who all get along perfectly.
想想让十五个人都融洽相处有多难，更不用说五十个人。
1:2: But unlike in friendships, you need coworkers.
但与朋友关系不同，你需要同事。
1:3: You work with them every day, and you depend on them just as they depend on you.
你每天与他们工作，依赖他们，正如他们也依赖你。
1:4: Here are some ways that you can get the whole office on your side.
下面这些方法能帮助你赢得整个办公室的支持。
2:0: If you have a bone to pick with someone in your workplace, you may try to stay tight-lipped around them.
如果你对某位同事有意见，也许会在对方面前守口如瓶。
2:1: But you won't be helping either one of you.
但这样对你们双方都没好处。
2:2: A Harvard Business School study found that observers consistently rated those who were upfront about themselves more highly, while those who hid lost trustworthiness.
哈佛商学院一项研究发现，观察者一贯更高地评价坦诚介绍自己的人，而隐藏自己信息的人会失去可信度。
2:3: The lesson is not that you should make your personal life an open book, but rather, when given the option to offer up details about yourself or studiously stash them away, you should just be honest.
教训并不是必须公开全部私生活，而是：在可以透露自己的细节或刻意藏起它们时，应选择诚实。
3:0: Just as important as being honest about yourself is being receptive to others.
愿意接受他人，与对自己诚实同样重要。
3:1: We often feel the need to tell others how we feel, whether it's a concern about a project, a stray thought, or a compliment.
我们常想告诉别人自己的感受，不论是对项目的担忧、一个偶然想法，还是一句赞美。
3:2: Those are all valid, but you need to take time to hear out your coworkers, too.
这些都合理，但你也要花时间听完同事的话。
3:3: In fact, rushing to get your own ideas out there can cause colleagues to feel you don't value their opinions.
事实上，急着表达自己的想法，可能让同事觉得你不重视他们的意见。
3:4: Do your best to engage coworkers in a genuine, back-and-forth conversation, rather than prioritizing your own thoughts.
尽量与同事展开真诚、有来有往的对话，而不是把自己的想法放在首位。
4:0: It's common to have a "cubicle mate" or special confidant in a work setting.
在工作环境中，有一个亲近的邻座同事或特别信赖的知己很常见。
4:1: But in addition to those trusted coworkers, you should expand your horizons and find out about all the people around you.
但除了这些可信的同事，你也应拓展交往范围，了解身边所有人。
4:2: Use your lunch and coffee breaks to meet up with colleagues you don't always see.
利用午餐与喝咖啡的休息时间，见见那些不常碰面的同事。
4:3: Find out about their lives and interests beyond the job.
了解他们工作之外的生活与兴趣。
4:4: It requires minimal effort and goes a long way.
这只需少量努力，却会有很大作用。
4:5: This will help to grow your internal network, in addition to being a nice break in the work day.
它既能拓展内部人脉，也能为工作日带来一段愉快的休息。
5:0: Positive feedback is important for anyone to hear.
每个人都需要听到积极反馈。
5:1: And you don't have to be someone's boss to tell them they did an exceptional job on a particular project.
你不必是某人的上司，也可以告诉他，在某个项目上表现出色。
5:2: This will help engender good will in others.
这有助于使对方对你产生好感。
5:3: But don't overdo it or be fake about it.
但不要过度，也不要虚假。
5:4: One study found that people responded best to comments that shifted from negative to positive, possibly because it suggested they had won somebody over.
一项研究发现，人们对从负面转向正面的评论回应最好，可能因为这使他们觉得自己已经赢得对方认可。
6:0: This one may be a bit more difficult to pull off, but it can go a long way to achieving results.
这一条可能较难做到，但能大大帮助取得成果。
6:1: Remember in dealing with any coworker what they appreciate from an interaction.
与任何同事交往时，都要记住，对方看重从互动中获得什么。
6:2: Watch out for how they verbalize with others.
留意他如何与其他人说话。
6:3: Some people like small talk in a meeting before digging into important matters, while others are more straightforward.
有人喜欢开会时先寒暄、再谈要事，另一些人则更直接。
6:4: Jokes that work on one person won't necessarily land with another.
对一个人奏效的笑话，不一定对另一个人也有用。
6:5: So, adapt your style accordingly to type.
因此，要按对方类型调整自己的风格。
6:6: Consider the person that you're dealing with in advance and what will get you to your desired outcome.
事先想想你在与谁打交道，以及什么方式能带来你想要的结果。

0:0: How to disagree with someone more powerful than you
如何与比你更有权力的人表达不同意见。
1:0: Your boss proposes a new initiative you think won't work.
上司提出一项新举措，你觉得它行不通。
1:1: Your senior colleague outlines a project timeline you believe is unrealistic.
资深同事列出一份项目时间表，你认为它不现实。
1:2: What do you say when you disagree with someone who has more power than you do?
与比你更有权力的人意见不同时，该怎么说？
1:3: How do you decide whether it's worth speaking up?
如何判断是否值得开口？
1:4: And if you do, what exactly should you say?
如果决定说，究竟该说什么？
1:5: Here's how to disagree with someone more powerful than you.
下面介绍如何向更有权力的人表达异议。
2:0: You may decide it's best to hold off on voicing your opinion.
你也许决定，最好先别说出自己的意见。
2:1: Maybe you haven't finished thinking the problem through, or you want to get a clearer sense of what the group thinks.
可能你还没把问题想透，或想更清楚了解群体的看法。
2:2: If you think other people are going to disagree, too, you might want to gather your army first.
如果认为其他人也会反对，可以先争取支持。
2:3: People can contribute experience or information to your thinking-all the things that would make the disagreement stronger or more valid.
他人的经验或信息能帮助你思考，让异议更有力、更有依据。
2:4: It's also a good idea to delay the conversation if you are in a meeting or other public space.
如果正在开会或身处其他公共场所，推迟交流也是好主意。
2:5: Discussing the issue in private will make the powerful person feel less threatened.
私下讨论问题，会让有权力的人觉得较少受到威胁。
3:0: Before you share your thoughts, think about what the powerful person cares about-it may be the credibility of their team or getting a project done on time.
分享想法前，考虑对方在意什么：也许是团队信誉，也许是按时完成项目。
3:1: You're more likely to be heard if you can connect your disagreement to a higher purpose.
如果能把异议与更高层次的目的联系起来，你更可能被听见。
3:2: When you do speak up, don't assume the link will be clear.
开口时，不要假定对方自然能看清这种联系。
3:3: You'll want to state it overtly, contextualizing your statements so that you're seen not as a disagreeable subordinate but as a colleague who's trying to advance a common objective.
应明确说出联系、交代发言背景，让人看见你不是爱唱反调的下属，而是在推动共同目标的同事。
3:4: The discussion will then become more like a chess game than a boxing match.
这样，讨论会更像一盘棋，而不是拳击赛。
4:0: This step may sound overly deferential, but it's a smart way to give the powerful person psychological safety and control.
这一步也许听起来过分恭顺，却能聪明地给对方心理安全感与控制感。
4:1: You can say something like, "I know we seem to be moving toward a first-quarter commitment here.
你可以这样说：“我知道，我们似乎准备作出第一季度的安排。
4:2: I have reasons to think that won't work.
我有理由认为这样行不通。
4:3: I'd like to lay out my reasoning.
我想说明自己的理由。
4:4: Would that be OK?"
可以吗？”
4:5: This gives the person a choice, allowing him to verbally opt in.
这给了对方选择，让他能口头表示愿意听。
4:6: And, assuming he says yes, it will make you feel more confident about voicing your disagreement.
假设对方答应了，你也会更有信心说出异议。
5:0: You might feel your heart racing or your face turning red, but do whatever you can to remain neutral in both your words and actions.
也许你心跳加速、脸红，但尽量让言语与行为保持中性。
5:1: When your body language communicates reluctance or anxiety, it undercuts the message.
身体语言若传达出不情愿或焦虑，就会削弱你的表达效果。
5:2: It sends a mixed message,and your counterpart gets to choose what signals to read.
它会发出混杂信号，让对方自行选择如何理解。
5:3: Deep breaths can help,as can speaking more slowly and deliberately.
深呼吸会有帮助，更慢、更沉稳地说话也会有帮助。
5:4: When we feel panicky, we tend to talk louder and faster.
惊慌时，我们常说得更响、更快。
5:5: Simply slowing the pace and talking in an even tone helps the other person cool down and does the same for you.
放慢节奏、保持平稳语调，能让对方冷静，也让你自己冷静。
5:6: It also makes you seem confident, even if you aren't.
这还会让你显得有信心，即使心里未必如此。
6:0: Emphasize that you're only offering your opinion, not gospel truth.
强调你只是在提出意见，而不是不可质疑的真理。
6:1: It may be a well-informed, well-researched opinion, but it's still an opinion, so talk tentatively and slightly understate your confidence.
即使意见经过充分了解与研究，它仍是意见，所以要用试探性的语气，稍微收敛确信。
6:2: Instead of saying: "If we set an end-of-quarter deadline, we will never make it," say, " This is just my opinion, but I don't see how we will make that deadline."
别说“定在季末截止，我们肯定完不成”，而说“这只是我的看法，但我不明白我们怎样能赶上这个期限”。
6:3: Having asserted your opinion (as a position, not as a fact),demonstrate equal curiosity about other views.
表达意见时，把它作为立场而非事实；随后也应同样好奇其他人的观点。
6:4: Remind the person that this is your point of view, and then invite critique.
提醒对方这只是你的视角，然后邀请批评。
6:5: Be open to hearing other opinions.

0:0: How to Get Active Again
如何重新开始活动。
1:0: Getting back into exercise can be a challenge in the best of times, but with gyms and in-person exercise classes off-limits to many people these days, it can be tricky to know where to start.
即使在最好的情况下，重新锻炼也可能是挑战；如今许多人无法使用健身房或参加线下课程，更难知道从哪里开始。
1:1: And it's important to get the right dose of activity.
活动量合适也很重要。
1:2: "Too much too soon either results in injury or burnout," says Mary Yoke, PhD, a faculty member in the kinesiology department at Indiana University in Bloomington.
印第安纳大学布卢明顿分校运动学教师玛丽·约克说：“太多、太快，可能造成受伤或耗竭。”
1:3: The following simple strategies will help you return to exercise safely after a break.
下面这些简单策略，能帮助你在中断后安全地恢复锻炼。
2:0: Don't try to go back to what you were doing before your break.
不要试图立刻恢复中断前的活动量。
2:1: If you were walking 3 miles a day, playing 18 holes of golf three times a week, or lifting 10-pound dumbbells for three sets of 10 reps, reduce activity to half a mile every other day, or nine holes of golf once a week with short walks on other days, or use 5-pound dumbbells for one set of 10 reps.
如果原来每天走三英里、每周三次打十八洞高尔夫，或用十磅哑铃做三组、每组十次，可以改为隔天走半英里、每周打一次九洞并在其他日子短走，或用五磅哑铃做一组十次。
2:2: Increase time, distance, and intensity gradually.
逐渐增加时长、距离与强度。
2:3: "This isn't something you can do overnight," says Keri L. Denay, MD, lead author of a recent American College of Sports Medicine advisory that encourages Americans to not overlook the benefits of activity during the pandemic.
近期美国运动医学会建议的主要作者、医生凯里·德奈说：“这不是一夜之间能做到的事。”该建议鼓励美国人不要忽视疫情期间运动的益处。
2:4: But you will reap benefits such as less anxiety and improve sleep right away.
不过，减轻焦虑、改善睡眠等好处，你可以立即获得。
3:0: If you're breathing too hard to talk in complete sentences, back off.
如果喘得不能完整说一句话，就降低强度。
3:1: If you feel good, go a little longer or faster.
如果感觉良好，可以稍微延长时间或加快速度。
3:2: Feeling wiped out after a session?
一次锻炼后筋疲力尽？
3:3: Go easier next time.
下次就轻松一些。
3:4: And stay alert to serious symptoms, such as chest pain or pressure, severe shortness of breath or dizziness, or faintness, and seek medical attention immediately.
还要警惕严重症状，例如胸痛或胸部压迫感、严重气短、眩晕或将要晕倒的感觉；出现这些情况，应立即寻求医疗帮助。
4:0: Consistency is the key to getting stronger and building endurance and stamina.
规律坚持，是变强和增强耐力、持久力的关键。
4:1: Ten minutes of activity per day is a good start, says Marcus Jackovitz, DPT, a physical therapist at the University of Miami Hospital.
迈阿密大学医院物理治疗师马库斯·杰科维茨说，每天活动十分钟是很好的起点。
4:2: All the experts we spoke with highly recommend walking because it's the easiest, most accessible form of exercise.
接受采访的专家都强烈推荐步行，因为它最容易开展，也最方便做到。
4:3: Although it can be a workout on its own, if your goal is to get back to Zumba classes, tennis, cycling, or any other activity, walking is also a great first step.
步行本身可以是一次锻炼；如果目标是重新参加尊巴课、网球、骑行或其他活动，它也是很好的第一步。
5:0: Even if you can't yet do a favorite activity, you can practice the moves.
即使暂时还不能做自己喜爱的活动，也可以练习动作。
5:1: With or without a club or racket, swing like you're hitting the ball.
有球杆或球拍也好，没有也好，都可以像击球那样挥动。
5:2: Paddle like you're in a kayak or canoe.
像坐在皮划艇或独木舟中一样划桨。
5:3: Mimic your favorite swimming strokes.
模仿自己喜欢的泳姿。
5:4: The action will remind you of the joy the activity brought you and prime your muscles for when you can get out there again.
这些动作会让你想起活动带来的快乐，也让肌肉为再次开展活动做好准备。
6:0: Exercising with others "can keep you accountable and make it more fun, so you're more likely to do it again," Jackovitz says.
杰科维茨说，与他人一起锻炼“能让你保持责任感，也更有趣，因此更可能再次去做”。
6:1: You can do activities such as golf and tennis or take a walk with others and still be socially distant.
你可以与别人打高尔夫、网球或散步，同时保持社交距离。
6:2: But when you can't connect in person, consider using technology.
不能当面交流时，可以考虑借助技术。
6:3: Chat on the phone with a friend while you walk around your neighborhood.
在社区散步时，与朋友打电话聊天。
6:4: FaceTime with a relative as you strength train or stretch at home.
在家力量训练或拉伸时，与亲人视频。
6:5: You can also join a livestream or on-demand exercise class.
也可以参加直播或点播运动课。

0:0: Think about driving a route that's very familiar.
想一想，开车走一条你非常熟悉的路线是什么情形。
0:1: It could be your commute to work, a trip into town or the way home.
它可能是你上班的通勤路线、进城的一段路，或回家的路。
0:2: Whichever it is, you know every twist and turn like the back of your hand.
无论是哪条路线，你都对每一个拐弯了如指掌。
0:3: On these sorts of trips it's easy to lose concentration on the driving and pay little attention to the passing scenery.
走这类路线时，人很容易在驾驶中走神，也很少留意沿途的景色。
0:4: The consequence is that you perceive that the trip has taken less time than it actually has.
结果就是：你觉得这趟行程用时比实际用时更短。
0:5: This is the well-travelled road effect: People tend to underestimate the time it takes to travel a familiar route.
这就是“熟路效应”：人们往往会低估走一条熟悉路线所需要的时间。
0:6: The effect is caused by the way we allocate our attention.
这种效应是由我们分配注意力的方式造成的。
0:7: When we travel down a well-known route, because we don't have to concentrate much, time seems to flow more quickly.
走一条熟悉的路线时，因为不必太专注，我们就觉得时间过得更快。
0:8: And afterwards, when we come to think back on it, we can't remember the journey well because we didn't pay much attention to it.
事后回想这段行程时，我们又记不太清，因为当时没有给予它太多注意。
0:9: So we assume it was shorter.
于是，我们便以为这趟行程耗时更短。

0:0: The supermarket is designed to lure customers into spending as much time as possible within its doors.
超市的布局旨在吸引顾客尽可能长时间地待在店内。
0:1: The reason for this is simple: The longer you stay in the store, the more stuff you'll see, and the more stuff you see, the more you'll buy.
原因很简单：你在店里待得越久，看到的东西就越多；看到的东西越多，买的也就越多。
0:2: And supermarkets contain a lot of stuff.
而超市里确实有大量商品。
0:3: The average supermarket, according to the Food Marketing Institute, carries some 44,000 different items, and many carry tens of thousands more.
据食品营销协会统计，一家普通超市经营的商品约有四万四千种，许多超市还要多出数万种。
0:4: The sheer volume of available choice is enough to send shoppers into a state of information overload.
可供选择的商品数量如此庞大，足以让购物者陷入信息过载。
0:5: According to brain-scan experiments, the demands of so much decision-making quickly become too much for us.
脑部扫描实验表明，如此大量的决策需求很快就会超出我们的承受能力。
0:6: After about 40 minutes of shopping, most people stop struggling to be rationally selective, and instead begin shopping emotionally - which is the point at which we accumulate the 50 percent of stuff in our cart that we never intended buying.
购物约四十分钟后，大多数人不再努力理性挑选，而开始凭情绪购物；就在这时，购物车里会堆起那一半我们原本没打算买的东西。

0:0: My dream has always been to work somewhere in an area between fashion and publishing.
我的梦想一直是在时尚与出版之间的某个领域工作。
0:1: Two years before graduating from secondary school, I took a sewing and design course thinking that I would move on to a fashion design course.
中学毕业前两年，我上了一门缝纫与设计课程，当时想着以后会接着学习服装设计。
0:2: However, during that course I realized I was not good enough in this area to compete with other creative personalities in the future, so I decided that it was not the right path for me.
然而，在上那门课时，我意识到自己在这个领域的能力不足以在未来与其他有创意的人竞争，因此认定这条路并不适合我。
0:3: Before applying for university I told everyone that I would study journalism, because writing was, and still is, one of my favourite activities.
申请大学之前，我告诉所有人自己会读新闻学，因为写作过去是、现在也仍然是我最喜欢的活动之一。
0:4: But, to be honest, I said it, because I thought that fashion and me together was just a dream - I knew that no one could imagine me in the fashion industry at all!
但说实话，我之所以那样说，是因为我觉得自己与时尚联系在一起不过是个梦——我知道根本没人能想象我会进入时尚行业！
0:5: So I decided to look for some fashion-related courses that included writing.
于是，我决定寻找一些包含写作内容的时尚相关课程。
0:6: This is when I noticed the course "Fashion Media & Promotion."
也就在这时，我注意到了“时尚传媒与推广”这门课程。

0:0: A fifth grader gets a homework assignment to select his future career path from a list of occupations.
一个五年级男孩拿到一项家庭作业：从职业清单中选择自己未来的职业方向。
0:1: He ticks "astronaut" but quickly adds "scientist" to the list and selects it as well.
他勾选了“宇航员”，却又很快把“科学家”添进清单，并且也选了它。
0:2: The boy is convinced that if he reads enough, he can explore as many career paths as he likes.
男孩深信，只要读得足够多，他想探索多少种职业道路，就能探索多少种。
0:3: And so he reads - everything from encyclopedias to science fiction novels.
于是他什么都读——从百科全书到科幻小说，无所不读。
0:4: He reads so passionately that his parents have to institute a "no reading policy" at the dinner table.
他读书读得如此入迷，以至于父母不得不规定：吃饭时不许看书。
0:5: That boy was Bill Gates, and he hasn't stopped reading yet - not even after becoming one of the most successful people on the planet.
那个男孩就是比尔·盖茨；直到今天他仍没有停止阅读，甚至在成为世界上最成功的人之一后也是如此。
0:6: Nowadays, his reading material has changed from science fiction and reference books: recently, he revealed that he reads at least 50 nonfiction books a year.
如今，他的阅读内容已不再局限于科幻小说和参考书；最近他透露，自己每年至少读五十本非虚构类书籍。
0:7: Gates chooses nonfiction titles because they explain how the world works.
盖茨选择非虚构类书籍，因为这些书能解释世界是如何运转的。
0:8: "Each book opens up new avenues of knowledge to explore", Gates says.
盖茨说：“每一本书都会为我们打开探索新知识的途径。”

0:0: It is easy to underestimate English writer James Herriot.
人们很容易低估英国作家詹姆斯·赫里奥特。
0:1: He had such a pleasant, readable style that one might think that anyone could imitate it.
他的文风如此亲切、易读，以至于人们可能以为谁都能模仿。
0:2: How many times have I heard people say, "I could write a book.
我不知多少次听人说过：“我也能写一本书。
0:3: I just haven't the time."
只是我没时间罢了。”
0:4: Easily said.
说起来容易。
0:5: Not so easily done.
做起来却没那么容易。
0:6: James Herriot, contrary to popular opinion, did not find it easy in his early days of, as he put it, "having a go at the writing game".
与人们通常的看法相反，赫里奥特在早期——用他自己的话说，开始“尝试写作这行”时——并不觉得写作容易。
0:7: While he obviously had an abundance of natural talent, the final, polished work that he gave to the world was the result of years of practicing, re-writing and reading.
尽管他显然天赋充沛，但最终呈献给世界的成熟作品，仍是多年练习、修改和阅读的成果。
0:8: Like the majority of authors, he had to suffer many disappointments and rejections along the way, but these made him all the more determined to succeed.
和大多数作家一样，他一路上不得不经历许多失望与退稿，但这些反而让他更加坚定了成功的决心。
0:9: Everything he achieved in life was earned the hard way and his success in the literary field was no exception.
他一生的每项成就都是艰苦努力换来的，文学上的成功也不例外。

0:0: It's almost impossible to go through life without experiencing some kind of failure.
人的一生几乎不可能完全不经历任何失败。
0:1: But, the wonderful thing about failure is that it's entirely up to us to decide how to look at it.
不过，失败有一个可贵之处：如何看待它，完全由我们自己决定。
0:2: We can choose to see failure as "the end of the world".
我们可以选择把失败看作“世界末日”。
0:3: Or, we can look at failure as the incredible learning experience that it often is.
也可以把失败看作一种难得的学习经历——它往往确实如此。
0:4: Every time we fail at something, we can choose to look for the lesson we're meant to learn.
每当我们做某件事失败，都可以选择寻找自己应从中学到的教训。
0:5: These lessons are very important; they're how we grow, and how we keep from making that same mistake again.
这些教训非常重要：我们靠它们成长，也靠它们避免再犯同样的错误。
0:6: Failures stop us only if we let them.
只有我们任由失败阻挡自己时，它才会让我们止步。
0:7: Failure can also teach us things about ourselves that we would never have learned otherwise.
失败还能让我们认识到自身的一些特质；若没有失败，我们本来永远不会了解这些。
0:8: For instance, failure can help you discover how strong a person you are.
比如，失败可以帮你发现自己究竟有多坚强。
0:9: Failing at something can help you discover your truest friends, or help you find unexpected motivation to succeed.
某件事上的失败，可以帮你认清谁才是真正的朋友，也可能让你找到意想不到的动力去争取成功。

0:0: We tend to think that friends and family members are our biggest sources of connection, laughter, and warmth.
我们往往认为，朋友和家人最能给我们带来联结、欢笑与温暖。
0:1: While that may well be true, researchers have also recently found that interacting with strangers actually brings a boost in mood and feelings of belonging that we didn't expect.
尽管这很可能属实，研究者最近也发现，与陌生人交流确实能改善心情、增添归属感，而这是我们没有预料到的。
0:2: In one series of studies, researchers instructed Chicago-area commuters using public transportation to strike up a conversation with someone near them.
在一系列研究中，研究者要求芝加哥地区乘坐公共交通的通勤者，主动与身边的人交谈。
0:3: On average, participants who followed this instruction felt better than those who had been told to stand or sit in silence.
平均来看，照做的参与者心情更好，胜过那些被要求安静站着或坐着的人。
0:4: The researchers also argued that when we shy away from casual interactions with strangers, it is often due to a misplaced anxiety that they might not want to talk to us.
研究者还指出，我们回避与陌生人的随意交流，往往是因为一种多余的担忧：怕对方不想与我们说话。
0:5: Much of the time, however, this belief is false.
然而，大多数时候，这种想法并不属实。
0:6: As it turns out, many people are actually perfectly willing to talk - and may even be flattered to receive your attention.
事实证明，很多人其实十分愿意交谈，甚至会因你主动关注他们而感到荣幸。

0:0: Although we try our best, sometimes our paintings rarely turn out as originally planned.
尽管我们尽了最大努力，有时画出来的作品仍很难达到原先设想的效果。
0:1: Changes in the light, the limitations of your painting materials, and the lack of experience and technique mean that what you start out trying to achieve may not come to life the way that you expected.
光线变化、绘画材料的局限，以及经验与技巧的不足，都会使你最初试图达到的效果，未必能按预期呈现出来。
0:2: Although this can be frustrating and disappointing, it turns out that this can actually be good for you.
虽然这种情况会让人沮丧、失望，但事实证明，它其实也可能对你有益。
0:3: Unexpected results have two benefits: you pretty quickly learn to deal with disappointment, and realise that when one door closes, another opens.
意外的结果有两项好处：你会很快学会应对失望，也会明白，一扇门关闭时，另一扇门就会打开。
0:4: You also quickly learn to adapt and come up with creative solutions to the problems the painting presents, and thinking outside the box will become your second nature.
你也会很快学会适应，并为绘画中遇到的问题想出有创意的解决办法；跳出固有思维，也会逐渐成为你的自然习惯。
0:5: In fact, creative problem-solving skills are incredibly useful in daily life, with which you're more likely to be able to find a solution when a problem arises.
事实上，有创意地解决问题的能力在日常生活中非常有用；凭借这些能力，遇到问题时，你更有可能找到解决办法。
